hops.afterHeading: The fibre that prefers a caress
hops.title: Fifty years from a cat's leg to a human forehead
hops.text: In 1939, the Swedish physiologist Yngve Zotterman recorded from a nerve serving the hairy skin of a cat's leg and caught slow, unmyelinated C fibres firing to gentle stroking. Similar fibres turned up in nonhuman primates, yet in 1990 Magnus Nordin could still write that they had not been proven to exist in people. In that paper he described sliding a tungsten electrode into a forehead nerve in human volunteers. Eight slow C fibres answered touches lighter than a quarter of a gram. A slow sweep of cotton wool drove them briskly, and rapid strokes made them fire less. The cat's gentle-touch fibres had been in human skin all along.

sources.citation: Moore et al., Journal of Physiology (2025), 603(16):4593-4608 (citing Zotterman, 1939, and Nordin, 1990).

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A tabby cat resting on a wooden bench as a puff of white cotton wool brushes its back, with an old oscilloscope in the background.
image.caption: Slow touch fibres recorded in a cat in 1939 were described in detail in human skin in 1990.

hops.afterHeading: Take the input away: what people show
hops.title: Your own stroke versus a friend's
hops.text: Close your eyes and slowly stroke the hairy back of your left forearm with your right hand, taking about three seconds to cross ten centimetres. Then, eyes still closed, have a friend copy the stroke and notice how the two feel. In 2019, Rebecca Boehme and colleagues compared self-stroking with strokes from an experimenter who mimicked each volunteer's motion. Another person's touch activated the insula and somatosensory cortex; self-touch deactivated the insula. On average, feeling a light filament press took nearly three times the force during self-stroking as during the experimenter's strokes, and over a hundred times the force with no stroking. Whose hand made the stroke mattered.

sources.citation: Boehme, Hauser, Gerling, Heilig & Olausson, PNAS (2019), 116(6):2290-2299.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: Two students at a wooden table, one gently stroking the back of the other's forearm while the recipient keeps their eyes closed.
image.caption: Self-stroking quieted the insula and made a light press harder to feel than another person's stroke did.

hops.afterHeading: From skin to reward-like outcomes in mice
hops.title: Dairy cows pushing a weighted gate to reach a brush
hops.text: A cow cannot fill in a pleasantness scale, so Emilie McConnachie and colleagues in British Columbia analyzed ten Holsteins trained to push a weighted gate. From seven kilograms, they added weight until no cow pushed through, though the final brush round ended early. Behind the gate was a mechanical brush that rotated on contact, fresh feed, or an empty space. The cows pushed similar weights for the brush and fresh feed, though under different test setups, and significantly less for the empty space. The gate records the heaviest load a cow opens; a mouse's place preference tracks change in time spent in a chamber. Neither shows how a touch feels.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A black-and-white dairy cow leaning contentedly against a large yellow rotating barn brush behind a weighted wooden gate.
image.caption: Holstein cows pushed similar gate weights to reach a brush as to reach fresh feed.
